questions.q: Which of the following is a molecular solid?
questions.explanation: Solid CO₂ consists of discrete molecules held by weak van der Waals forces.

questions.q: What is the coordination number of an atom in hexagonal close packing (hcp) or cubic close packing (ccp)?
questions.explanation: Each sphere touches 6 in its own layer, 3 above and 3 below, giving 12.

questions.q: Alkali halide crystals heated in the vapour of the alkali metal acquire colour. The colour is due to:
questions.explanation: Excess metal atoms create anion vacancies occupied by electrons, which absorb visible light.

questions.q: In a close-packed lattice of N atoms, the numbers of octahedral and tetrahedral voids are respectively:
questions.explanation: There is one octahedral void and two tetrahedral voids per atom.

questions.q: Atoms of element B form a ccp lattice and atoms of A occupy two-thirds of the octahedral voids. The formula of the compound is:
questions.explanation: For N atoms of B there are N octahedral voids, so A = 2N/3. A : B = 2/3 : 1 = 2 : 3.

questions.q: A cubic crystal of an element has molar mass 52 g/mol, density 7.2 g cm⁻³ and edge 289 pm (N_A = 6.022 x 10²³). Its unit cell is:
questions.explanation: Z = dN_A a³/M = 7.2 x 6.022 x 10²³ x (2.89 x 10⁻⁸)³/52 ≈ 2.0, which is bcc.

questions.q: What is a Frenkel defect? Name one compound that shows it and give one effect on the crystal.
questions.answer: In a Frenkel defect a smaller ion (usually the cation) leaves its lattice site and occupies an interstitial site. It is shown by AgBr, AgCl or ZnS. The density of the crystal remains unchanged.
keyPoints: Smaller ion moves to an interstitial position
questions.explanation: No ions leave the crystal in a Frenkel defect, only change position.

questions.q: A metal crystallises in an fcc lattice with edge length 400 pm. Calculate the radius of the metal atom.
questions.answer: In fcc, atoms touch along the face diagonal: 4r = √2 a, so r = a/(2√2) = 400/2.828 ≈ 141 pm.
questions.explanation: The face diagonal of the cube passes through three atoms in contact.

questions.q: Which of the following is a colligative property?
questions.explanation: Colligative properties depend on the number of solute particles; depression of freezing point is one of them.

questions.q: The sum of the mole fractions of all components in a solution is:
questions.explanation: Mole fractions are fractions of the total number of moles, so they add up to 1.

questions.q: What is the osmotic pressure of a 0.01 mol/L solution of a non-electrolyte at 300 K? (R = 0.0821 L atm mol⁻¹ K⁻¹)
Two solutions are isotonic when they have the same:
options: osmotic pressure at the same temperature
questions.explanation: Isotonic solutions exert equal osmotic pressure at a given temperature, so there is no net flow across a semipermeable membrane.

questions.q: 10 g of a non-volatile solute (molar mass 100 g/mol) is dissolved in 250 g of water. Taking K_b of water as 0.52 K kg mol⁻¹, the elevation of boiling point is:
Four aqueous solutions each of molality 0.1 m are listed. Assuming complete dissociation of electrolytes, which has the highest boiling point?
questions.explanation: CaCl₂ gives 3 particles (i = 3), more than NaCl (2) or the non-electrolytes (1), so it has the largest elevation.

questions.q: What is an azeotrope?
questions.answer: An azeotrope is a liquid mixture that boils at a constant temperature and distils over with the same composition as the liquid, so its components cannot be separated by fractional distillation.
keyPoints: Liquid and vapour have the same composition; cannot be separated by fractional distillation
questions.explanation: Azeotropes arise from large deviations from Raoult's law.

questions.q: Calculate the mole fraction of ethanol in a solution of 4.6 g ethanol (C₂H₅OH, 46 g/mol) in 36 g of water (18 g/mol).
questions.answer: Moles of ethanol = 4.6/46 = 0.1; moles of water = 36/18 = 2.0. Mole fraction of ethanol = 0.1/(0.1 + 2.0) = 0.1/2.1 ≈ 0.048.
questions.explanation: Mole fraction is moles of the component divided by total moles.

questions.q: What is the function of a salt bridge in a galvanic cell?
options: It completes the circuit and maintains electrical neutrality of the two solutions
It supplies electrons to the cathode
It increases the EMF of the cell
questions.explanation: Ions migrate through the salt bridge to balance the charge built up in the half-cells.

questions.q: Which of the following is a secondary cell?
questions.explanation: A lead storage battery can be recharged, so it is a secondary cell.

questions.q: During discharge of a lead storage battery, the density of the sulphuric acid electrolyte:
questions.explanation: H₂SO₄ is consumed to form PbSO₄ and water is produced, so the solution becomes less dense.

questions.q: When a solution of a strong electrolyte is diluted, its molar conductivity:
questions.explanation: On dilution ions move more freely with less inter-ionic attraction, so Λm rises towards its limiting value.

questions.q: Iron pipelines are protected by connecting them to blocks of magnesium because:
options: magnesium is less reactive than iron
magnesium forms a thick oxide layer on iron
magnesium is oxidised in preference to iron and acts as a sacrificial anode
magnesium makes the iron a cathode of an electrolytic cell
questions.explanation: Mg has a more negative electrode potential, so it corrodes instead of iron.

questions.q: In the electrolysis of concentrated aqueous sodium chloride (brine), the product liberated at the cathode is:
questions.explanation: Water is reduced more easily than Na⁺, so H₂ is formed at the cathode (and Cl₂ at the anode).

questions.q: Write the electrode reactions and the overall reaction of the alkaline hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell.
keyPoints: Anode: hydrogen oxidised in presence of OH⁻
questions.explanation: The fuel cell converts chemical energy directly into electrical energy.

questions.q: The conductivity of a 0.1 mol/L KCl solution is 0.0129 S cm⁻¹. Calculate its molar conductivity.
keyPoints: Λm = κ x 1000 / c (c in mol L⁻¹)
Substitute κ = 0.0129 S cm⁻¹ and c = 0.1
questions.explanation: 1000/c converts the volume per mole into cm³.

questions.q: The rate law of a reaction is expressed in terms of:
options: the stoichiometric coefficients of the balanced equation only
the molecularity of the overall reaction
concentrations of reactants raised to powers determined experimentally
questions.explanation: The powers in the rate law (the orders) are found from experiment and need not equal the coefficients.

questions.q: A reaction whose rate does not depend on the concentration of the reactant has an order of:
questions.explanation: For a zero-order reaction, rate = k[A]⁰ = k, which is constant.

questions.q: A plot of ln k against 1/T is a straight line whose slope is:
questions.explanation: ln k = ln A − E_a/(RT), so the slope is −E_a/R and the intercept is ln A.

questions.q: For a zero-order reaction, the half-life is:
options: inversely proportional to the initial concentration
directly proportional to the initial concentration
proportional to the square of the initial concentration
questions.explanation: For zero order, t½ = [A]₀/2k, so it is proportional to [A]₀.

questions.q: In a reaction the concentration of the reactant falls from 0.8 M to 0.4 M in 20 minutes and from 0.4 M to 0.2 M in the next 20 minutes. The order of the reaction is:
questions.explanation: A constant half-life (20 min) independent of concentration is the characteristic of a first-order reaction.

questions.q: A zero-order reaction has k = 0.01 mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹ and an initial concentration of 0.5 mol L⁻¹. The time taken for the reactant to be completely consumed is:
questions.explanation: For zero order, [A] = [A]₀ − kt, so t = 0.5/0.01 = 50 s.

questions.q: What are pseudo first-order reactions? Give an example.
questions.answer: A reaction that is actually of higher molecularity but behaves as first order because one reactant is present in large excess, so its concentration is practically constant. Example: acid-catalysed hydrolysis of ethyl acetate (excess water) or inversion of cane sugar.
keyPoints: One reactant is in large excess, its concentration is constant
Example such as hydrolysis of ester or inversion of sucrose
questions.explanation: The excess reactant's concentration is absorbed into the rate constant.

questions.q: A first-order reaction has k = 2.303 x 10⁻² min⁻¹. How long does it take for 90% of the reactant to be consumed?
questions.explanation: Since 2.303/k = 100 min and log 10 = 1, the time is 100 min.

questions.q: Smoke is a colloidal system of:
options: a gas dispersed in a liquid
a liquid dispersed in a gas
a solid dispersed in a gas
a solid dispersed in a liquid
questions.explanation: Smoke consists of fine solid particles dispersed in air; it is an aerosol.

questions.q: Milk is a colloidal system classified as:
questions.explanation: Milk has fat droplets dispersed in water.

questions.q: Brownian movement of colloidal particles is caused by:
options: the electric charge on the particles
bombardment of the particles by molecules of the dispersion medium
questions.explanation: Unbalanced collisions with the medium's molecules make the particles move in a zig-zag path, which also keeps the sol stable.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of heterogeneous catalysis?
options: Hydrolysis of an ester with dilute HCl
Combination of N₂ and H₂ over iron in the Haber process
Oxidation of SO₂ with NO in the lead-chamber process
Decomposition of an ester in aqueous acid
questions.explanation: Here the catalyst (solid iron) is in a different phase from the gaseous reactants.

questions.q: At very high pressure the extent of adsorption of a gas on a solid becomes independent of pressure. In the Freundlich equation x/m = kP^(1/n) this corresponds to 1/n being:
questions.explanation: When 1/n = 0, P⁰ = 1, so x/m = k and adsorption is constant (saturation).

questions.q: A catalyst whose selectivity depends on the pore structure and on the size and shape of the reactant and product molecules is called a:
questions.explanation: Zeolites are shape-selective catalysts, because only molecules that fit the pores can react or leave.

questions.q: What is electrophoresis? What does it show about a colloidal sol?
questions.answer: Electrophoresis is the movement of colloidal particles towards one of the electrodes under an applied electric field. It shows that colloidal particles carry an electric charge.
keyPoints: Movement of colloidal particles in an electric field
Particles move towards the oppositely charged electrode
Proves that colloidal particles are charged
questions.explanation: The direction of migration shows the sign of the charge.

questions.q: Why does the extent of physisorption of a gas decrease when the temperature is raised?
questions.answer: Adsorption is exothermic (ΔH is negative). By Le Chatelier's principle, raising the temperature favours the reverse process (desorption), and the weak van der Waals forces cannot hold the gas molecules at higher thermal energy.
keyPoints: Le Chatelier: higher temperature favours desorption
Weak van der Waals forces are overcome by thermal motion
questions.explanation: Physisorption is generally high at low temperature.

questions.q: Which noble gas is used for filling weather balloons because it is light and non-inflammable?
questions.explanation: Helium is the second lightest gas and does not burn.

questions.q: Bleaching powder is represented by the formula:
questions.explanation: Bleaching powder is made by passing chlorine over slaked lime and is represented as CaOCl₂ (Ca(OCl)Cl).

questions.q: Which catalyst is used in the Contact process for the manufacture of sulphuric acid?
questions.explanation: V₂O₅ catalyses the oxidation of SO₂ to SO₃.

questions.q: What is the hybridisation of sulphur in SF₆?
questions.explanation: Six bond pairs and no lone pair give an octahedral shape with sp³d² hybridisation.

questions.q: Among HClO, HClO₂, HClO₃ and HClO₄, the strongest acid is:
questions.explanation: More oxygen atoms disperse the negative charge of the anion better, so the acid strength increases with oxidation state of chlorine.

questions.q: The H–N–H bond angle in NH₃ (about 107°) is larger than the H–P–H angle in PH₃ (about 94°) because:
options: phosphorus is larger, so its lone pair is more spread out
nitrogen is more electronegative, so bond pairs lie nearer to N and repel more
PH₃ has no lone pair on phosphorus
questions.explanation: Bond pairs close to the central atom repel each other more strongly, widening the angle; in PH₃ they lie farther from P.

questions.q: Write the equation for the industrial manufacture of ammonia by Haber's process and state the conditions.
questions.answer: N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), ΔH = −46.1 kJ/mol. Conditions: iron catalyst with promoters, about 200 atm pressure and about 700 K.
keyPoints: High pressure (about 200 atm) and about 700 K
questions.explanation: High pressure favours ammonia; moderate temperature balances yield and rate.

questions.q: Why is HF a weak acid in water while HCl is a strong acid?
questions.answer: The H–F bond is very strong (high bond enthalpy), so HF ionises only slightly. HF molecules and F⁻ ions are also strongly hydrogen bonded, which limits ionisation, whereas the weaker H–Cl bond breaks easily.
keyPoints: H–F bond is much stronger than H–Cl
Hence HF ionises only to a small extent
questions.explanation: Acid strength of hydrogen halides increases from HF to HI.

questions.q: Brass is an alloy of copper and:
questions.explanation: Brass is Cu + Zn; bronze is Cu + Sn.

questions.q: The colour of an acidified solution of potassium dichromate (K₂Cr₂O₇) is:
questions.explanation: Dichromate ions are orange; chromate ions are yellow.

questions.q: The electronic configuration of chromium (Z = 24) is:
questions.explanation: A half-filled d subshell is extra stable, so one 4s electron shifts to give 3d⁵4s¹.

questions.q: Which of the following 3d-series elements shows the highest oxidation state of +7?
questions.explanation: Manganese can use all its 3d and 4s electrons (3d⁵4s²), giving +7 as in KMnO₄.

questions.q: In acidic medium, one mole of MnO₄⁻ oxidises how many moles of Fe²⁺?
questions.explanation: MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O accepts 5 electrons, and each Fe²⁺ gives 1.

questions.q: Which ion has the maximum number of unpaired electrons?
questions.explanation: Fe³⁺ is d⁵ with 5 unpaired electrons; Fe²⁺ has 4, Co²⁺ has 3 and Cu²⁺ has 1.

questions.q: What are interstitial compounds? State two of their characteristics.
questions.answer: Interstitial compounds are formed when small atoms such as H, C or N occupy the interstitial voids in the metal lattice. They are generally very hard, have high melting points, are chemically inert and retain metallic conductivity.
keyPoints: Small atoms (H, C, N) trapped in the voids of the metal lattice
Very hard with high melting points
questions.explanation: Examples are TiC and Fe₃H.

questions.q: Explain why Mn³⁺ is a strong oxidising agent while Cr²⁺ is a strong reducing agent.
questions.answer: Mn³⁺ (d⁴) readily gains an electron to form the stable half-filled d⁵ ion Mn²⁺. Cr²⁺ (d⁴) readily loses an electron to form Cr³⁺ (d³, t₂g³), which is very stable.
keyPoints: Cr²⁺ → Cr³⁺ gives stable t₂g³ configuration
Stability of the product drives oxidising or reducing behaviour
questions.explanation: Both ions are d⁴ but their products are particularly stable.

questions.q: In Werner's theory the secondary valence of a metal corresponds to its:
questions.explanation: Secondary valence is non-ionisable and equals the coordination number; primary valence is the oxidation state.

questions.q: What is the oxidation state of copper in [Cu(NH₃)₄]²⁺?
questions.explanation: NH₃ is neutral, so the charge on the metal equals the charge of the complex ion, +2.

questions.q: The formula of tetraamminedichloridocobalt(III) chloride is:
questions.explanation: Co³⁺ with 4 NH₃ and 2 Cl⁻ gives a +1 complex cation, balanced by one chloride.

questions.q: The denticity of the ligand EDTA⁴⁻ is:
questions.explanation: EDTA binds through two nitrogen and four oxygen donor atoms, so it is hexadentate.

questions.q: How many geometrical isomers are possible for the square planar complex [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂]?
questions.explanation: The two Cl ligands can be adjacent (cis) or opposite (trans).

questions.q: Excess AgNO₃ is added to a solution containing 1 mole of [Co(NH₃)₅Cl]Cl₂. How many moles of AgCl precipitate?
questions.explanation: Only the two ionisable chloride ions outside the coordination sphere precipitate; the coordinated Cl⁻ does not.

questions.q: Write the IUPAC names of (i) [Ni(CO)₄] and (ii) K₂[PtCl₄].
questions.explanation: Ligands are named first, then the metal with its oxidation state.

questions.q: Explain why aqueous solutions of Cu²⁺ complexes are coloured but those of Zn²⁺ are colourless.
questions.answer: Cu²⁺ (d⁹) has a partially filled d subshell, so d–d transitions by absorption of visible light are possible and a complementary colour is seen. Zn²⁺ (d¹⁰) has a completely filled d subshell, so no d–d transition can occur and it is colourless.
keyPoints: Cu²⁺ is d⁹ and has a vacancy in d orbitals
Zn²⁺ is d¹⁰, no d–d transition
questions.explanation: Colour in complexes arises from d–d electronic transitions.

questions.q: The common name of CHCl₃ is:
questions.explanation: CHCl₃ is trichloromethane, commonly called chloroform.

questions.q: Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) released into the atmosphere mainly damage the:
questions.explanation: In the stratosphere CFCs release chlorine atoms that catalytically destroy ozone.

questions.q: Which alkyl bromide reacts fastest by the S_N2 mechanism?
questions.explanation: S_N2 is fastest at the least hindered carbon, i.e. methyl, followed by primary, secondary and tertiary.

questions.q: Methyl bromide reacts with sodium metal in dry ether to give:
questions.explanation: Wurtz reaction: 2CH₃Br + 2Na → CH₃–CH₃ + 2NaBr.

questions.q: 2-Bromobutane is heated with alcoholic KOH. According to Saytzeff's rule the major product is:
questions.explanation: Elimination gives the more substituted, more stable alkene, but-2-ene.

questions.q: A racemic mixture is optically inactive because:
options: its molecules have a plane of symmetry
the equal and opposite rotations of the two enantiomers cancel each other
the enantiomers combine to form a meso compound
questions.explanation: A racemate has equal amounts of d and l forms, so net rotation is zero (external compensation).

questions.q: What is meant by an ambident nucleophile? Give one example.
questions.answer: An ambident nucleophile can attack through either of two different atoms, for example the cyanide ion (through C or N) or the nitrite ion (through N or O).
keyPoints: Nucleophile with two possible attacking sites
Gives two different products depending on the site
questions.explanation: The site of attack depends on the reaction conditions and the reagent.

questions.q: An alkyl halide gives an alkyl cyanide with KCN but an isocyanide with AgCN. Explain.
questions.answer: KCN is ionic and gives free CN⁻ ions, which attack through carbon (forming the stronger C–C bond) to give R–CN. AgCN is covalent, so only the nitrogen lone pair is available for attack, giving R–NC.
keyPoints: KCN is ionic: attack through carbon gives R–CN
AgCN is covalent: attack through nitrogen gives R–NC
questions.explanation: The nature of the cyanide salt decides which atom acts as the nucleophile.

questions.q: Methanol is also known as:
questions.explanation: Methanol was originally obtained by destructive distillation of wood.

questions.q: Commercial ethanol is denatured mainly to:
questions.explanation: Poisonous or foul-tasting substances (methanol, pyridine) are added so it cannot be misused as a beverage.

questions.q: Acid-catalysed hydration of propene gives mainly:
questions.explanation: Water adds according to Markovnikov's rule, so –OH goes to the middle carbon.

questions.q: A primary alcohol can be oxidised to the aldehyde without going further to the acid by using:
questions.explanation: PCC is a mild oxidising agent that stops at the aldehyde stage.

questions.q: Which of the following is the most acidic?
questions.explanation: The –NO₂ group withdraws electrons and stabilises the phenoxide ion, whereas the –CH₃ group in p-cresol destabilises it.

questions.q: Anisole on heating with concentrated HI gives:
questions.explanation: The O–CH₃ bond cleaves because the C(aryl)–O bond is strong (partial double bond character) and does not break.

questions.q: Write the equation for the dehydration of ethanol to ethene and state the conditions.
questions.answer: CH₃CH₂OH → CH₂=CH₂ + H₂O, on heating with concentrated H₂SO₄ at about 443 K.
keyPoints: Temperature about 443 K (at 413 K ether forms instead)
questions.explanation: Intramolecular dehydration occurs at the higher temperature.

questions.q: Why is o-nitrophenol more acidic than o-methoxyphenol?
questions.answer: The –NO₂ group is electron-withdrawing; it disperses the negative charge of the phenoxide ion and stabilises it. The –OCH₃ group is electron-releasing and intensifies the negative charge, destabilising the phenoxide ion.
keyPoints: –NO₂ withdraws electrons and stabilises the phenoxide ion
A more stable conjugate base means a stronger acid
questions.explanation: Substituents affect acidity through their influence on phenoxide stability.

questions.q: What is the IUPAC name of CH₃CHO?
questions.explanation: A two-carbon aldehyde is ethanal (acetaldehyde).

questions.q: The IUPAC name of acetone is:
questions.explanation: Acetone, CH₃COCH₃, is propanone.

questions.q: Which of the following does not reduce Fehling's solution?
questions.explanation: Aromatic aldehydes such as benzaldehyde do not reduce Fehling's solution; aliphatic aldehydes do.

questions.q: Which compound gives a yellow precipitate of iodoform when warmed with I₂ and NaOH?
questions.explanation: Compounds containing a CH₃CO– group (methyl ketones) give the iodoform reaction; propanone has this group.

questions.q: Ethanoic acid heated with Cl₂ in the presence of red phosphorus (Hell–Volhard–Zelinsky reaction) gives:
questions.explanation: The α-hydrogen is replaced by chlorine, giving ClCH₂COOH.

questions.q: Sodium ethanoate is heated with soda lime (NaOH + CaO). The main product is:
questions.explanation: Decarboxylation removes CO₂: CH₃COONa + NaOH → CH₄ + Na₂CO₃.

questions.q: What is the Etard reaction?
questions.answer: Toluene is oxidised with chromyl chloride (CrO₂Cl₂) in CS₂ to form a chromium complex, which on hydrolysis gives benzaldehyde.
questions.explanation: The reaction stops at the aldehyde and does not give benzoic acid.

questions.q: Why are aldehydes more reactive than ketones towards nucleophilic addition?
questions.answer: In aldehydes the carbonyl carbon is attached to one alkyl group and one hydrogen, so there is less steric hindrance and less electron-donating (+I) effect, making the carbon more electrophilic. In ketones two bulky alkyl groups hinder attack and reduce the positive charge on carbon.
keyPoints: Only one electron-donating alkyl group, so carbonyl carbon is more positive
questions.explanation: Steric and electronic effects both favour aldehydes.

questions.q: Aniline is an example of:
questions.explanation: Its –NH₂ group is attached directly to a benzene ring.

questions.q: Aqueous solutions of aliphatic amines are:
questions.explanation: Amines accept protons from water, producing OH⁻ ions.

questions.q: Ethanamide (CH₃CONH₂) is treated with Br₂ and aqueous NaOH (Hofmann bromamide reaction). The product is:
questions.explanation: The amine formed has one carbon atom less than the amide.

questions.q: Aniline reacts with bromine water to give:
questions.explanation: The –NH₂ group strongly activates the ring, giving a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromoaniline.

questions.q: Which gas is evolved when ethylamine reacts with nitrous acid (NaNO₂ + HCl)?
questions.explanation: Aliphatic primary amines give unstable diazonium salts that decompose to the alcohol and nitrogen gas.

questions.q: In Hinsberg's test, which type of amine gives a sulphonamide that is insoluble in aqueous alkali?
questions.explanation: The sulphonamide of a secondary amine has no acidic N–H hydrogen, so it stays insoluble; that of a primary amine dissolves in alkali.

questions.q: Write the equation for the reaction of ethylamine with ethanoyl chloride.
questions.answer: C₂H₅NH₂ + CH₃COCl → CH₃CONHC₂H₅ + HCl, forming N-ethylethanamide. A base such as pyridine removes the HCl.
keyPoints: HCl is formed and removed by a base
questions.explanation: Primary and secondary amines undergo acylation.

questions.q: Why is aniline not nitrated directly with a nitrating mixture to give mainly the para product?
questions.answer: In the strongly acidic mixture aniline is protonated to the anilinium ion, which is meta-directing, giving a large amount of meta-nitroaniline. Aniline is also oxidised by nitric acid, forming tarry products.
keyPoints: Aniline is protonated to the anilinium ion
Oxidation by nitric acid causes tar
questions.explanation: Protecting the amino group by acetylation avoids these problems.

questions.q: Which of the following is a non-reducing sugar?
questions.explanation: In sucrose the reducing groups of glucose and fructose are tied up in the glycosidic bond, so it does not reduce Tollens' or Fehling's reagent.

questions.q: The main storage polysaccharide in plants is:
questions.explanation: Plants store glucose as starch; animals store it as glycogen.

questions.q: Enzymes are mostly:
questions.explanation: Enzymes are globular proteins that act as biological catalysts.

questions.q: How many chiral carbon atoms are present in the open-chain structure of glucose?
questions.explanation: Carbons 2, 3, 4 and 5 each carry four different groups.

questions.q: α-D-Glucose and β-D-glucose are anomers that differ in the configuration at carbon number:
questions.explanation: Anomers differ at the new chiral centre (C-1) created on ring closure of the aldehyde group.

questions.q: How many hydrogen bonds join a guanine–cytosine base pair in DNA?
questions.explanation: G–C pairs have three hydrogen bonds, while A–T pairs have two.

questions.q: What are vitamins? Name the two broad groups with one example of each.
questions.answer: Vitamins are organic compounds required in small amounts for normal growth and health that the body cannot make in sufficient quantity. They are fat-soluble (A, D, E, K) or water-soluble (B group, C).
keyPoints: Organic compounds needed in small amounts
questions.explanation: Solubility determines whether a vitamin is stored in the body.

questions.q: Amino acids have high melting points and are soluble in water but insoluble in non-polar solvents. Explain.
questions.answer: In the solid and in neutral solution an amino acid exists as a zwitterion (dipolar ion), H₃N⁺–CHR–COO⁻. The strong ionic attractions give high melting points, and the ionic character makes them soluble in polar water but not in non-polar solvents.
keyPoints: Strong electrostatic forces give high melting points
Ionic nature gives solubility in water, not in non-polar solvents
questions.explanation: The proton moves from the –COOH group to the –NH₂ group, forming a dipolar ion.
